extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, regulators, and policymakers considering rulemaking reform
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate and design rulemaking procedures so that the delay (ossification) they cause is neither reflexively condemned nor uncritically preserved but set at an optimal level that balances its costs and benefits. Focus is on when to add, retain, or relax procedural requirements for different kinds of rulemakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimize ossification (weigh delay's costs and benefits)
rubrics_metrics.description: The goal should not necessarily be to reduce ossification but rather to optimize it: "the goal should be to maximize the benefits of delay while minimizing its costs." Evaluate reforms by accounting for (a) the traditional benefits and costs of regulatory procedures (e.g., scientific accuracy, prevention of arbitrariness) and (b) the benefits and costs produced by delay itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating proposals for reform, do not simply say 'ossification' is bad; instead enumerate and net out the direct benefits of procedures and the independent benefits of delay (commitment value; legitimacy) against their costs (slower promulgation, resource diversion). Consider the entire mix of procedures and how each contributes to delay and quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess need for credible commitment (ossification as commitment mechanism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ossification can be valuable when agencies need to make commitments durable because regulated parties will only undertake long-term investments or behavior if they reasonably expect rules to persist. "Ossification makes change more difficult... regulated parties can have relatively greater confidence that regulations that now exist will continue to exist."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the rule creates incentives requiring long-term stability (e.g., incentive programs, schemes that induce capital investment). If regulated actors face large upfront costs whose recoupment depends on regulatory durability, stronger procedural safeguards (and thus more delay) may be justified. By contrast, rules aimed at stopping immediate dangers do not usually require such commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess delay's contribution to agency legitimacy and public acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Delay may increase public understanding and acceptance of important rules: "ossification allows the public time to more fully understand what is happening and respond." This can bolster agency legitimacy and public confidence in regulatory durability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether rulemaking would benefit from allowing information to disseminate across diverse publics (information asymmetries) and whether increased public engagement/time would improve perceived legitimacy. Give greater procedural weight to politically contentious or culturally significant rules where legitimacy gains are likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor procedural intensity to rule characteristics (rule-level tailoring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking procedures should vary depending on whether the rule at issue benefits from credible commitments or legitimacy concerns. "Rulemaking procedures should vary depending on whether the rule at issue falls in one of the categories for which credible commitments are especially valuable."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer tailoring at the individual rule level (rather than agency-wide), because a single agency may promulgate both rules that benefit from delay and those that do not. Identify criteria for heightened procedures (e.g., long-term incentives, political significance) and apply more onerous procedures selectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use administrable significance thresholds (economic/significance lines)
rubrics_metrics.description: One administrable approach is to require additional procedures for especially expensive or significant regulations (e.g., the Congressional Review Act's 'major' rule definition or EO 12,866's 'significant' regulatory action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using monetary or 'significance' thresholds (e.g., $100 million) is administrable though imperfect—both over- and underinclusive. It can serve as a starting line for which rules get heightened procedures but anticipate gaming and exceptions for culturally sensitive items that may not be economically large.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design to minimize agency evasion/gaming
rubrics_metrics.description: When procedural intensity is tied to thresholds, agencies may attempt to evade by splitting or structuring rules to fall below the threshold. "Agency evasion must also be accounted for... the agency will simply divide regulations into smaller rules."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate and guard against evasion (e.g., by substantive aggregation rules, anti-splitting doctrines, or oversight). Recognize that any bright-line will create cat-and-mouse dynamics and plan enforcement/monitoring accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimentation and empirical evaluation before large-scale reform
rubrics_metrics.description: We lack sufficient data to fine-tune optimal ossification. The Article urges targeted experimentation and the collection of empirical evidence (e.g., trial runs, randomized assignment of some rules to formal tracks) to learn costs and benefits. "Finding optimal ossification almost certainly will involve targeted experimentation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement controlled pilot programs (e.g., randomly assign a subset of expensive rules to formal rulemaking) and systematically measure time, cost, quality, private-sector responses, and legitimacy outcomes. Use experiments to identify which procedures produce net benefits before broad adoption or repeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and measure each procedure's contribution to delay and quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Optimization requires knowing how much each individual procedure contributes to ossification and whether that contribution is justified by the procedure's benefits. "We do not have much data... how much each individual procedure contributes to that ossification."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audit procedures (e.g., Portland Cement disclosure, material-comment responses, OIRA review, NEPA analyses, cross-examination) to estimate marginal delay and marginal quality gains. Target reforms at procedures whose costs exceed their benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider adding targeted heightened procedures for especially costly or important rules
rubrics_metrics.description: For regulations that particularly benefit from commitment or legitimacy (and are expensive or significant), consider adding specific procedures such as cross-examination, more comprehensive OIRA cost-benefit review, or additional expert scrutiny to improve quality and deliberately slow change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For 'especially expensive' rules, evaluate whether intensive procedural tools (e.g., cross-examination of agency experts, court-reviewable OIRA analyses) would produce net gains in commitment value and legitimacy that justify added delay and cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve expedited good-cause exception for immediate dangers
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is real and immediate danger, expedited procedures should remain available (APA good-cause exception). "The APA already draws this sort of line through its 'good cause' exception, which allows an agency to use expedited procedures when there is a real danger."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retain a narrow and enforceable 'good cause' pathway to bypass ordinary procedural delays when urgency or imminent harm justifies faster action. Use this as the inverse rule to ossification-heavy tracks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require meaningful disclosure to facilitate public comment (Portland Cement principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: An NPRM should turn over the data or formulas an agency intends to use so interested persons can comment meaningfully. (Portland Cement doctrine: studies relied upon must be available during rulemaking.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandate disclosure of supporting studies/data for significant rule proposals to enable substantive public input. Recognize this increases procedural burden and time but improves meaningfulness of comments and the credibility of the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to material/significant comments proportionally
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should respond to all 'material' or 'significant' comments, which promotes public involvement but increases procedural burden and time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define materiality thresholds to focus agency responses on comments that bear significantly on the rule's substance; for highly material comments, require substantive responses to support later judicial review. For lower-stakes rules, consider more limited response obligations to save time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for judicial review incentives (hard-look effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard-look (arbitrary-and-capricious) judicial review incentivizes agencies to take many procedural steps before finalizing rules to avoid invalidation, which can lengthen rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering reforms, account for how changing standards of judicial review (e.g., greater deference or different review tests) would alter agencies' ex ante procedural investments and thus overall ossification. Balance the risk that easing review reduces careful deliberation ('agency sloppiness') against the benefit of reduced delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose between status-quo, targeted increases, or reallocation of procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Three policy options are (1) retain current mix of procedures; (2) increase procedures for categories of rulemakings especially benefited by credible commitments; or (3) increase procedures for some categories while reducing them for others. "Picking between Options 1, 2, and 3 is difficult without having a better... sense of costs and benefits."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical evidence and pilot experimentation to choose among these options. Prefer approaches that are administrable and minimize gaming while achieving net social benefits.
